# React Conventions

## Components and Props

- **A module exports exactly one component**, with its props type at most, and is named for it. The
  helper components it needs stay in that file, unexported, so no other module can reach them. A
  module exporting two — a navigation shell that also exports a toggle and a menu — is two modules.
- **Components that belong together go in a folder named for their area, one file each**, published
  through the area's index as the TypeScript rules' **Area Imports** describe. The folder holds
  components that each earn their place under the next bullet; it never shelters one that is
  another's variant or a hook's wrapper. A client component's `"use client"` directive goes on the
  first line of its own file.
- **A shared UI library is primitives and the fuller components built from them, and a difference in
  look or behavior is a prop or variant on its owner, never another component.** A primitive is one
  layout, type, surface or control with variants — a stack, a text, a panel, a button — taking
  children but no named slots and opening no portal. A fuller component — a page, a section, a
  dialog, a list, a form — composes primitives and takes slots, as the structure bullet below says.
  A component that renders one other component with some of its look or behavior props fixed or
  defaulted, and adds no content, data or state of its own, is that owner's variant: a
  `DangerNotice` rendering `<Notice tone="danger" dismissible={false}>` is `tone="danger"` on
  `Notice`. One that only runs a hook and renders nothing or its children is that hook, called where
  it is needed, unless it carries the `"use client"` boundary for a Server Component call site. A
  chain of components each adding one prop or value is one component with variants, counted from the
  call site to the primitive at its end. A variant shares its owner's structure; a branch that
  renders a different tree is a second component behind a prop, and becomes that component.
- Named exports for components
- Default exports only for page components

- Destructure props in function signature
- Use optional chaining for optional props
- Provide sensible defaults

```typescript
function Card({ title, action, footer, children, variant = "default" }: CardProps) {
  // ...
}
```

- **A component owns its structure; a call site supplies content.** A surface made of parts — a
  card with a title, an action, a body and a footer — is one exported component that takes them as
  slots (`action={...}`, `footer={...}`, `children`) and owns their spacing, alignment, dividers and
  type sizes through its variants, so each kind of text — a name, a figure, a label — has one size
  across the product. A slot takes the element itself — `action={<Button>…</Button>}`, never
  `actionLabel` and `actionHref` — so each caller keeps its own content without the component
  growing a prop per field. Its parts — a header, a body, a title, an item — are unexported helpers
  in its file: exported compound parts (`Panel`, `PanelHeader`, `PanelBody`), however common in
  component libraries and pattern guides, the `vercel-composition-patterns` and
  `tailwind-design-system` skills' compound examples included, are the hand-assembly this forbids.
  A call site fills slots; it never assembles the surface from parts or primitives, and structural
  behavior a caller needs becomes a prop or variant. Where a surface is hand-assembled or exports
  its parts, the fix names the one component that replaces it and lists each slot prop it takes.
- **Layout and type come from primitives, never from class strings.** A feature component arranges
  its content with the shared layout and text primitives — a row, a column, a grid, a box, a text, a
  heading — through their variants (`<Flex gap="sm" justify="between">`, `<Type size="sm"
  tone="muted">`), never a `className` spelling out flex, gap, padding, color or type size. A raw
  utility class is allowed only for positioning, animation, an override a third-party component
  needs, or a width on a layout primitive; a button keeps its own, as **Rendering and Events** says.
  A case the primitives cannot express becomes a new variant on the primitive
  that owns it, never a class string at the call site, so one spacing and type scale holds everywhere.
  These allowances belong to the code that builds the UI; an app built on a shared UI library takes
  none of them, as the next bullet says.
- **An app built on a shared UI library writes no styling of its own.** No `className`, no
  class-merging call such as `cn(`, no class string kept in a constant or a style module, no style
  rule or styled component of its own — its stylesheet only loads the library's — and no inline
  `style` except a value read from saved data, such as a column width the reader dragged and saved.
  Each page is a tree of the library's components configured by their props and variants, so every
  page looks standard: a page reads
  `<Section title="Favorites" description="…"><Stack gap="md">…</Stack></Section>`, never a `div`
  spelling out the section's padding and border. A case the library cannot express becomes a prop or
  variant on the shared component that owns it, never a local wrapper, and no shared component takes
  a `className` prop that would let a caller reach around its variants.
- **Responsive layout is the primitive's own CSS.** A primitive changes layout with the room it is
  given through the styling system's container variants, or its responsive variants where the
  viewport decides (`@md:` and `md:` in Tailwind), and a variant value says what it renders at every
  width — never a `cols={3}` whose classes collapse to one column at a breakpoint the caller cannot
  see, as the `tailwind-design-system` skill's grid example does. Script that must know the width
  reads the theme's breakpoint through one shared hook; a number restating a breakpoint, color or
  spacing step the theme declares is a second copy of that token.

## Reference Data

- **Reference data comes from a maintained package, never from a list typed into the repository.**
  Countries and their subdivisions, currencies, languages, time zones, dialling codes, bank and card
  networks, MIME types: each is a published standard somebody else already tracks, revises when it
  changes, and ships with types. Reach for the popular, well-maintained package first, and treat
  adding the dependency as the cheaper option, because it is.
- **A short hard-coded list is the failure mode, and it never reads like one.** Eight countries in a
  select looks like a sensible starting point and is in fact a silent limit on who can use the
  screen: the reader whose country is missing cannot finish the form, and nothing reports it. The
  same list then gets copied into the next form that needs it.
- Where a list genuinely has no package — a set this product defines, such as its own plans or
  statuses — it is declared once, in one module, with every consumer importing it. Two copies of one
  list is the defect, whatever the list is of.
- Judge a package on how widely it is used and how recently it was maintained, not on how small it
  is. Weigh the bytes it adds where the data is large and say in the pull request what it costs, but
  never trade completeness away to avoid the download.
- **Completeness is what the dependency buys, so use all of it.** Importing the package and then
  filtering it down to the handful of entries that seemed likely is the hard-coded list again, one
  layer along.

## Shared Surfaces

- **Verify shared controls in the rendered surface at every supported responsive mode.** Check
  each visible control's purpose, count, accessibility and behavior, including the computed styles
  that make alternative controls mutually exclusive. A DOM assertion or a capture of one intended
  change does not establish that the surrounding controls work; inspect the whole changed surface
  before accepting it, and fix duplicated or incorrectly visible controls at their shared owner.

- **Find the established owner before building a repeated surface.** When the same page section,
  navigation element, menu, input, loading state or action appears elsewhere, move the established
  implementation into a generic shared primitive. A local component built on the shared primitive
  supplies content — its own data and copy — and picks a documented variant at the call site; it
  never fixes a variant under a second name, as **Components and Props** says, and never recreates
  structure, styling, fetching or interaction behavior. An interface
  that is correct in one consumer is the canonical starting point for the extraction, not a visual
  reference to copy.

- **One shared page section owns initial loading and the content it reveals.** Its single
  noninteractive skeleton stays visible until every request needed for the initially visible
  heading, counts, controls and content resolves; a consumer cannot add a second loader or reveal
  structural content afterward. Keep the settled section mounted during background refresh and
  pagination, and show an explicit error when a required request fails. Validate the shared section
  with a cold load and a revalidation: the cold load changes directly from one complete skeleton to
  one complete section, and revalidation does not remove or append the section's visible structure.
- **A page states that something is missing only once its request has said so.** "Not found", an
  empty list or a "nothing here yet" state shows after the request answers with that result, such
  as a 404 or an empty page of results. While the request is pending, or before it has started,
  the skeleton is all the reader sees; data not arrived yet is never read as data that does not
  exist.
- **A click that navigates shows the destination at once, finished where the data could be loaded
  ahead.** Load a destination's data before the click whenever the reader signals where they are
  going: a pointer resting on a row or link, keyboard focus on it, or a link in view whose
  destination is cheap to load. Where each destination costs several requests, as a detail page
  opened from a list does, load it on that signal for the one row in question, never for every row
  on screen. The skeleton is the fallback for data that has not arrived by the click: the
  destination's frame and skeleton replace the current page at once, and the old page never stays
  on screen while the next one's requests run. Each route segment that waits on data owns its own
  loading boundary, so the fallback shows wherever the navigation diverges, and the destination
  starts its independent requests together rather than one after another. Validate it by timing a
  click to content after resting on the row, and a cold click to the skeleton and to the content,
  against a deliberately slowed backend.

- **A change to a shared mechanism is applied everywhere that mechanism appears, and on every
  sibling surface, in the same change.** A widget grid, a list row, a dialog shell, an edit-mode
  chrome, an empty state: when a fix arrives for one page built on it, the other pages built on it
  are in scope too. Whether a correction the user makes to how one page looks or reads reaches
  other pages is `pre-production`'s **Scope Follows The Defect, Not The Request** to decide.
  Search for every surface that renders the same component or hook before editing, and every
  sibling surface — the variants of one document, the create and edit of one record, the same
  surface built for two audiences — whether or not it renders that component yet, since siblings
  share one structure; land the change on all of them together. A page left on the old shape is a
  defect, not a follow-up.
- **A surface that does for one audience what another already does for a second takes that
  sibling's component, placement, size and controls, differing only in the content each audience
  needs.** A first-run checklist, a status summary or a
  setup step shown to each role, plan or workspace kind is one surface: when one audience's version
  sits in the grid at half width with plain rows, the other's is not a full-width card with its own
  buttons. Read the existing sibling before building the new one, and build on it.
- **A recurring interaction follows the product's established flow.** Before placing controls for
  selecting, changing or removing related items, inspect comparable screens for where the list,
  action and editing surface live. Keep the same division between viewing and editing unless the
  new task needs a different one; changing labels alone is not a reason to bury the interaction in
  an unrelated section or invent another control shape.
- Where a page genuinely cannot take the new shape, say which page and why in the pull request;
  silently leaving it behind is what turns a redesign into an inconsistency.

## Interface Copy

- **Write interface copy in American English**, in spelling and in vocabulary alike: a colour is a
  "color", a centre is a "center", and a person "enrolls" rather than "enrols". A reader meeting the other spelling reads it as a mistake, and a product that uses both
  reads as two products.
- **Headings, labels, buttons, tabs and menu items share one capitalization across the product**,
  sentence case unless the product has settled on another: "Save draft", "Shared folders", "Reading
  list". A mix is the defect; a proper noun keeps its own capitals. Capitalization is the source
  string's: a type variant that renders text uppercase is styling, and the string stays written in
  the product's case.

- **Write labels, descriptions and hints for someone who already trusts the product.** Copy that
  warns the reader about their own ordinary action reads as suspicion. A person submitting a record on
  behalf of someone in their own workspace, who has already ticked the box that says they may, does
  not need to be told that the action is logged or attributed to them.
- **Name a surface for what it holds, never for the reader's role in it.** A reader knows which role
  they hold, so "Organizer events", "Attendee tickets" or "Your speaker profile" labels them rather
  than the thing; the heading is "Events", "Tickets", "Profile", whatever the surface holds.
- **Every heading and title is a name in a word or a short phrase, never a sentence.** That holds
  for a page, a section, a card and a dialog, and for a state the page shows in place of its
  content, such as an empty state, an error or a refusal: "Overview", "Contact details", "No
  playlists yet", "Sync off". A sentence, such as "This folder is shared with you as read-only", or
  a phrase addressed to the reader, such as "What you can do here" or "Let's get you set up", goes
  in the line under the heading, which carries the explanation.
- **Features offered side by side carry names no reader could mistake for each other.** Each name
  says what the feature holds or does in the reader's words, so a reader who has used neither picks
  the right one: "Collections" beside "Groups", or "Profiles" beside "Accounts", reads as two words
  for one thing. Read the names together, as the reader meets them, before settling either.
- **A refusal is a short, friendly request for the reader's next step**, such as "Please choose a
  date after today." It says what to do rather than passing a verdict on what was done, and it
  never repeats back what the reader just entered or chose — a file name, a typed value, a picked
  item — which they already know. This holds wherever the message is written, an API's error
  message the interface shows included.
- **The interface writes its own text for a reason another reader's message carries.** A message a
  service writes for a different reader, such as an agent, an API client or a log, says what that
  reader needs: an agent's carries the URL it can follow. The service sends a reason code beside
  it, and the interface writes the words for its own reader and the page they are on, never
  showing the other reader's message.
- **Never write copy about the product's state that nobody has confirmed.** A page that says a
  feature is unavailable, coming soon or not yet supported, when nobody said so, misinforms the
  reader; the product's state is confirmed with the user before any copy states it.
- **Never state what the reader takes for granted.** That data is encrypted, stored securely, kept
  private, or handled carefully is assumed of any product in this category; saying it out loud plants
  the doubt it was meant to settle. Mention a property only where the reader has to act on it or
  where it departs from what they would assume.
- **Keep implementation out of the interface.** Storage, masking, hashing, background jobs, retries
  and the names of internal states belong in the code. A description says what the field is for and
  what the reader should put in it, in the words they would use themselves.
- **Every section, every step of a flow and every dialog carries a one-sentence description under
  its own heading, inside its surface** — two on a flow's first step, as **A flow starts at its
  first question** below allows — saying what the reader does there, what the section holds, or why
  the dialog appeared, in terms of what the reader is trying to do: "Choose how you hear about new
  activity", "The people who can see and edit this project", "Sharing an album requires a verified
  email address first." It never narrates the surface's own controls, such as "Pressing Next opens…"
  or "Click below to…": the button's label already names its action. A heading alone, or a heading
  with only a badge beside it, is the defect, in every state the surface renders, a loading or
  failed one included. A shared dialog component makes its description a required prop, so a
  title-only dialog cannot be written. No sentence floats between the page's top bar and its first
  section: a page's name sits where the product puts page titles, and whatever a page-level sentence
  would say belongs to the section it describes.
- **Spell out an abbreviation the reader may not know the first time a surface uses it**, with the
  short form after it, such as "Service Level Agreement (SLA)"; later mentions on that surface use
  the short form alone.
- Say the one thing the reader needs and stop. On a field, prefer no description to a description
  that repeats the label, narrates the obvious, or hedges, and keep out of any label what the
  product already knows about the reader, such as their own email address in a confirmation label.
  Where a sentence is only there to cover the product, cut it. That includes a paragraph explaining
  the mechanics around an action, such as which party performs which step, and a note of a side
  effect nobody asked about, such as what happens to earlier versions.
- **A dialog's commit button never repeats the label its trigger and title already carry.** The
  reader pressed "Add song" to open the dialog and read "Add song" as its title; a third "Add song"
  on the button says nothing new. The commit names the act in the fewest words: "Save" for a form
  that adds or changes something, the bare verb for a confirmation — "Delete" under "Delete
  playlist". When that verb is also the word the product's dialogs use to dismiss, such as "Cancel",
  the commit adds what it acts on — "Cancel booking" — so one word never means both doing the
  act and backing out of it.
- **A bare verb labels a control only where what it acts on is plain from what surrounds it**, as
  under a dialog's title. A control among several things it could act on names its object: "Shuffle
  queue" beside a player's search field and volume, never "Shuffle".
- **A list filter takes tabs only for a few top-level groups that fit one row on a phone**, such as
  all, mine and shared; a filter with more options, or one likely to gain them, such as a
  status, is a select in the filter bar. A row of many tabs wraps or scrolls on a phone and takes
  the room the next filter needs, while a select holds any number of options in one control. A
  filter select's options carry no counts; a count beside a filter option belongs only on a tab.
- **A status reads from the viewer's side.** Name the state in terms of what that reader did or
  still has to do, and keep internal steps they take no part in behind a visual cue: a person who
  sent a form sees "Submitted", with the tone telling review apart from acceptance, while the
  reviewer sees "Pending review" and "Approved". One status maps to each audience's label in one
  place.
- **A banner or notice about something not yet possible says what will make it possible, never
  that it is held back.** Its sentence names who has to do what and what that enables — "This
  member must confirm their email to enable exports" — rather than "Exports stay blocked until they
  confirm", which reads as a penalty. Words such as blocked, locked, denied, stay or until frame a
  pending step as a punishment; keep them for a refusal the reader can do nothing about. A status
  label or badge is not such a sentence: it names the state plainly, as the status bullet above
  says.

### Confirmation Dialogs

- **A dialog title names the action and is never a question.** "Archive record", "Delete role",
  "Discard draft": the title is what the reader is about to do, stated flatly, so it reads the same
  whether the dialog asks for confirmation or reports a result. "Archive record?" puts the
  question in the one place the reader cannot answer it.
- **The body is where the question is asked, and a confirmation body opens with "Are you sure you
  want to …".** After the question, one sentence on what follows — what the reader loses, what stops
  working, whether it can be undone — and nothing else. On a confirmation, this body is the
  dialog's description, and the question with its one consequence sentence stands in for the
  one-sentence limit.
- **The body never opens with the title again.** A title reading "Archive record" over a body
  reading "Archive Ann Lee? …" says the same words twice and spends the only line the reader
  actually reads on the one they have already read. Write the body as though the title is above it,
  because it is.
- Name the record in the title's noun, not the title's value: a dialog headed with one record's
  name is a different heading on every row, and the reader learns nothing from it that the row they
  clicked did not already tell them.
- **Typing to confirm is reserved for the most severe actions**, such as deleting an account or a
  whole workspace, where everything the reader holds goes at once. There the reader types something
  that identifies what they are acting on and the action stays unavailable until it matches. Every
  other action, including one that cannot be undone — deleting a record, removing a saved address,
  sending a message — is confirmed by the dialog's button alone.
  A phrase demanded for routine actions slows every one of them and is soon typed by reflex.
- One component owns this shape, under **Shared Surfaces** above: dialogs hand-built from the same
  primitives are where these rules get broken one at a time.

## Layout And Spacing

- **Text inside an application surface stays within the product's heading scale.** A section,
  card, panel or step title takes the size its component owns, under **Components and Props**
  above; a display-size headline, a hero line or marketing lettering inside an application surface
  outranks the page it sits on and reads as an advertisement. Display type belongs to marketing
  pages outside the application shell.
- **Read the padding on every screen the change touches, at every width it is checked at.** Content
  clipped by a header, text against a card's edge, a control overlapping the thing below it, a gap
  that collapses at one breakpoint: each is invisible in the diff and obvious on the screen, and
  each reaches the reader because nobody looked. Compare neighboring banners and sections as well:
  their content insets and the gaps between them must follow the same shared spacing scale. Fix
  inconsistent padding or gaps in the owning component rather than adding page-specific overrides.
- **Chrome positioned over content is the usual cause.** An absolutely positioned header, toolbar or
  footer takes no space, so whatever sits behind it is hidden with nothing in the markup to say so.
  Prefer giving that chrome its own row in a flex or grid column, where the browser reserves the
  space; reach for absolute positioning only where the overlap is the intent.
- **A page takes the content frame of its kind, and every page of that kind takes the same one.**
  The product's page layout has few frames, each set once in a layout component — commonly a
  centred column for a page the reader passes through to finish one task and then leaves, such as a
  step of a multi-step flow, a standalone form outside the navigation or a confirmation, and the
  full-width frame for a page reached from the navigation, whatever it holds. A page never sets its
  own width, centring or outer padding. Two pages of one kind whose content starts at different
  distances from the navigation read as two products.
- **A surface is as tall as its content, never taller.** A card, panel, section or widget showing a
  large empty area — below its content, or between the content and the control that acts on it —
  reads as unfinished. Content flows from the top; artificial filler never pushes a control to the
  bottom of a stretched container or the far edge of an otherwise empty row or footer. Surfaces the
  established layout already pairs in a row split its width evenly, unless
  one is a main area beside a narrow side rail. They end on the same line, and they get there by
  balancing what they hold — cutting a
  line that earns no place, moving a control, re-pairing the surfaces — never by stretching the
  shorter one; where content cannot be balanced, the shorter keeps its own height. An empty state is
  sized like any other content. Content that can outgrow its surface scrolls inside a
  maximum height, so the surface stays as tall as its content until it reaches the cap. A height set
  from outside the content belongs only to a surface whose content fills the space it is given — a
  chart, a map, media — to one the reader sized, or to a section deliberately sized to the viewport.
- **Size interactive content for its values, relationships and task, not a fixed fraction of the
  page.** Keep a page section's structural frame, heading, description and dividers at the width its
  page layout assigns. Bound simple control groups inside that frame so short values and their
  actions stay together; give structured content the room its columns and relationships need.
  Compact controls do not require a narrow container, and a wide container does not require
  stretched controls. Use the product's established layout and control sizes, preserving comparable
  widths under **Forms**, rather than shrinking the section or creating a new peer-section row.
- **Place actions by what they affect, beside the content they act on.** A page's own actions —
  create, import, a toggle into a mode such as reorder or bulk edit, and the strip that mode shows
  while it is on — sit directly above the content they act on, below the page's banners and its
  load-failure area. Never put them in the header bar, the top navigation, or anywhere else above
  the banners, where they are far from what they change and easy to miss. The page layout owns that
  order — banners, failures, actions, content — so no page renders its own toolbar above it. An
  action on one section or item stays with that section or item. Do not move a contextual action
  into a detached row merely to satisfy a width or proximity rule. At narrower widths, wrap or stack
  related content and controls while preserving readable values, visible context, accessible labels
  and a clear association with their actions.
- **A table row stacked on a narrow screen reads from the left.** Each value sits left-aligned
  under its column's label; only the row's "⋯" menu takes the right edge. A value pushed to the
  right edge reads as detached from its label and sends the eye zigzagging across the card.
- **A frame that scrolls shows its scrollbar whenever its content overflows** — a box of legal
  text, a dialog body, a list or a table inside a maximum height — on every platform and before the
  reader touches it, so cut-off text reads as more to scroll rather than as text that ends. A hidden
  or hover-only scrollbar on such a frame is the defect, including the overlay scrollbar a platform
  hides until scrolling, which the shared scroll component replaces with one it always renders. The
  scroll container is styled once, in that component or the product's base styles, never per call
  site. This holds over general advice to hide scrollbars for a cleaner look.
- **Navigation decides who reaches a page, and the decision that hides a page also refuses to serve
  it.** An address the viewer's role, workspace, plan or permissions never offer them redirects to
  the viewer's home. A feature a higher plan includes is offered, locked, as the plan bullet below
  says, never redirected. A screen or empty state telling the viewer the page belongs to somebody
  else — "this page is for …", "switch to … to use it", "you don't have access" — is dead code
  wherever it sits, in a page, a layout or a gate: the check becomes the redirect and the screen is
  deleted, never restyled, moved into a shared message component, or kept because a task lists it
  among the states to restyle.
- **Settings is the last group in the primary navigation, and the reader's own account is the last
  item within it.** The work the product exists for comes first; settings about the shared
  workspace come before settings about the reader themselves.
- **A multi-step flow the reader has finished — a verification, a setup, an onboarding — leaves the
  navigation, and its address redirects to the viewer's home.** A finished flow whose outcome is
  final shows no banner where the reader lands, a toast at most; one whose submission waits on
  someone else's decision — a review, an approval — lands the reader on the product as usual, with
  the banner the banner bullet below describes until the decision lands. A status page standing in
  the flow's place, at its own address or any other, is the defect. A page that a flow finished
  outside the product returns the reader to — the address an external service sends the reader back
  to once its own step is done — is that flow's last step and stays.
- **Inside a page, offer only what applies to the reader.** A choice, a document, a field or a
  status row the reader can never use — the other region's version of a document, the other account
  type's settings — is left out, decided by the same rule that decides which one applies, never
  listed beside it. What is left out is the item, never the step or section holding it: a step or
  section stays for every reader who still has something in it to answer, and goes only when nothing
  in it is left. A field whose value the context already fixes — the language of a course taught in
  only one, the venue of an event held in only one — is not asked: the value is set, and shown as
  text where the reader should know it.
- **A feature the reader's plan does not include is shown working, with its paid controls locked,
  never described by a notice.** The reader can start one, open it and see every option the paid
  plan adds, rendered as on that plan but disabled, and do what costs nothing, such as naming it and
  saving one with its defaults; the server refuses anything past that. Once the reader holds what
  their plan allows, the create action stays in place, disabled, with a hint on hover and focus that
  names the plan which creates more and links to the plans page, in the tooltip the next bullet
  describes. One notice in that surface names what upgrading unlocks, as the controls the reader
  can see, beside the upgrade action. A sentence saying the plan lacks the feature, or that the
  reader gets a default named by an internal term, shows nothing they would gain.
- **Every hover or focus hint uses the product's one tooltip, never a second popup built for one
  case.** A hint holding a link is that tooltip made reachable by pointer and keyboard: the reader
  can move into it and tab to the link.
- **A page's content offers one control per destination or action** — a button, a link, a menu item,
  an icon or a clickable row; the app's own navigation is not counted against it. Two that open the
  same form or page — a checklist step's button or linked label beside a quick link, a page action
  repeated inside the section below it — read as two different actions and crowd the page. Keep the
  one control where the reader looks for it; elsewhere, text naming the same destination stays plain
  text, and a control that carries nothing else is removed.
- **A row that opens its record is itself the control.** Clicking anywhere on a list or table row,
  or pressing Enter on it, opens or edits the record it shows; a pencil, "Edit" or "View" button
  beside it makes the reader find a second target for the one destination and is left out. Other
  controls in the row, such as the row's menu or a role picker, keep their own action without
  opening the row.
- **A row's actions go in one "⋯" menu at the row's end, not as buttons inline in the row.** Delete,
  archive, set as default, download and the like are menu items, with a destructive item last; a
  row of icon or text buttons competes with the row's content and differs from row to row. A
  control that is the row's content, such as a role picker or an on/off switch, stays in the row,
  and so does a remove control on an entry being edited in a form, such as one line of a list the
  reader is still writing.
- **An action graver than its neighbours is set apart from any action it could be mistaken for.**
  In a menu it goes last, below a divider; in a group of buttons it stands apart from the rest. Two
  destructive actions listed together, such as removing a member beside deleting the workspace, are
  one slip of the pointer apart, and the slip costs far more in one direction; sharing a red tone
  does nothing to tell them apart.
- **A field gets no button beside it for what editing it or leaving it already does.** An edit in
  place shows its save alone: Escape or moving away cancels it and keeps the saved value. A "×"
  button outside the field to cancel or clear it is a second control for the same thing, easy to
  mistake for a delete, and is left out; a clear "×" inside a search field, as part of the field, is
  the expected shape.
- **A flow starts at its first question.** A step that only introduces the product, lists what it
  offers or explains what comes next asks the reader for nothing and is removed. The context a
  first-time reader needs to answer that question — what they are creating and what it holds —
  stays, as one or two plain sentences in the first step's description; removing the step never
  removes the explanation. A flow left with one step is a single page, with no stepper. This holds
  over general onboarding advice to open with a welcome screen or a concept tour.
- **Every step of a multi-step flow renders as a page, in the flow's own chrome, never as a
  dialog.** A dialog is for one action taken from inside a page, however long its form —
  submitting a form outside any flow, submitting on someone's behalf, a quick edit — and one form
  serves the page and the dialog alike, inside each shell.
- **A record created from a short form is created in a dialog.** Its list's create button opens a
  dialog holding the form, such as a folder's name and icon; the list page never keeps the form open
  above its content, and the record gets no create page of its own. A create page is for a record
  whose form is a document the reader builds, such as a report with its sections.
- **A dialog is as wide as its content needs and no wider.** Take the smallest width on the
  product's dialog scale that holds its widest field or control group at its natural size, such as
  a row of icon choices; an empty band beside the content reads as unfinished and pushes the
  actions away from what they act on. When even the smallest step leaves a band, the scale gains a
  smaller step rather than the dialog a width of its own. Content that already spans the dialog,
  such as a grid of many options, keeps the width that lets the reader scan it, however much room
  each cell has to spare.
- **A dialog holds one form.** When the reader chooses between several forms or documents, the
  choice is made on the trigger before the dialog opens — a menu listing each option with a
  one-line description — never as tabs or a switcher inside it. A field the form itself submits,
  such as a type selector, is part of that form and stays inside.
- **A row of actions that follows content sits together, never spread to opposite edges.** On a
  page, such as a full-page form, a card or the choices under a prompt, the row starts where the
  content starts, at the bottom-left, with the primary action last. In a modal, a dialog or a
  confirmation, the row sits at the bottom-right, the primary action rightmost and cancel
  immediately to its left, where readers of modals look for them. A dialog that only points the
  reader to one next step, such as a prompt to complete a requirement before an action, shows that
  action alone: its "×" already closes it, and a cancel beside the step the product wants taken
  invites the reader away from it. A dialog that collects input, takes a purchase or confirms an
  action keeps its cancel. Actions are centred only under content that is itself centred, such as
  an empty state. A multi-step flow's footer is the one
  exception, as the next bullet says; a control beside a heading, in a toolbar, at the end of a
  table row or in a floating save panel follows that surface's own layout.
- **A multi-step flow's footer puts "Back", on every step that has one, at its start and the
  forward action at its end, apart; a footer holding only the forward action places it at the start,
  as no control sits alone at the far edge of an empty footer. It labels them by position, never by
  the step's content:** "Next" on every step before the last
  and "Submit" on the last, so the control that goes back never sits beside the one that commits.
  "Save address", "Continue", "Save and continue" or "Create profile" make each step's control look
  like a different action, and the step's heading already says what it holds. This holds for every
  page system that moves through steps — an onboarding, a setup, a verification, a wizard, a form
  split across pages — whether or not each step saves as it advances, and over general advice to
  name a button for its action.
- **"Next" only moves on; it never performs the step's work.** A step whose requirement is an action
  — linking an account, connecting a calendar, uploading a file — offers that
  action as its own button in the step's content, and "Next" stays disabled until the requirement
  is met. A forward control that opens a dialog, starts a connection or makes a change before it
  advances leaves the reader unable to tell moving on from acting, and a step that advances on its
  own once the action finishes takes the reader somewhere they did not ask to go.
- **Every page renders in the product's page layout, including a page that reports a state** — a
  confirmation, such as the return page a flow finished outside the product lands on, or an expired
  link — with its content in sections, each headed and described as **Interface Copy** says. A
  section carries what the reader needs next — the record the state concerns, its status, the action
  that moves on, in that section's footer. A confirmation also thanks the reader, marks the success,
  and says what they now have and what happens next — never a neutral status panel, nor a
  placeholder for something the reader does not have yet such as "appears here". It ends on one
  action, which returns the reader to the page they left to start the flow, or to their home when
  that is unknown. A label and a button centred in an otherwise empty page is the defect, and so is
  a small card left under chrome that no longer applies, such as tabs or a form header. The page for
  an address that does not exist is the exception: a full-page message centred in the screen,
  outside the navigation, with one action home. A notice that the page is for somebody else, and a
  status page standing in a finished flow's place, are deleted as the bullets above say.
- **A boxed banner appears only when the reader has something to do, something is wrong, or
  something they submitted is waiting on a decision** — terms to accept, a verification to finish,
  a load that failed, a blocking state to resolve, a submission under review, worded from the
  reader's side as **Interface Copy**'s status bullet says. **General information the reader need
  not act on takes the slim notice instead**: one line, a soft tint, no border or shadow — how many
  projects the reader's plan includes, a note on how a feature behaves. Weight follows whether the
  reader must act, never how important the message feels: information in a boxed banner, a
  bordered callout or a card reads as a demand, and a state the reader must act on in a slim notice
  is missed. A success or completed state shows neither, and a toast at most when the reader's own
  action just caused it. A dismissible "approved" or "done" banner, and whatever stores its
  dismissal, is the defect: delete both.
- **A toast reports a result of the reader's action that the page does not already show, or the
  completion of a flow** — a record saved, an invitation sent, a file exported. An action that
  changed nothing the reader can see closes without one: a request already recorded, a step only
  someone else can take, a save with nothing changed, a dialog's Continue after the dialog has said
  what happens next. Apart from the flow-completion toast below, a toast never repeats text the
  dialog or page already shows, and one that claims an outcome which did not happen, such as a
  notification nobody sent, is the worse defect. A step of a multi-step flow shows none when the
  reader moves on, since reaching the next step is the feedback; the action that completes the flow
  shows one, worded as its completion, even where the page it lands on says the same in a banner,
  which the reader may not see at once. A form's save stays disabled until something in it differs
  from what was loaded, so a save with nothing changed cannot be made.
- **A banner about the account or workspace, rather than the page, shows only on top-level pages**
  — the home page and each destination the primary navigation lists — never on a page nested below
  one, such as a record's detail, edit or create page or a step of a flow. Storage nearly full, a
  renewal coming due, a note about the plan: the reader meets them where they arrive, and a
  nested page keeps its space for the task in hand. The page's level in the navigation decides it,
  in one place, so a new nested page leaves the banner out without being listed. A banner that
  explains why the page's own actions are refused — a read-only or suspended workspace on a page
  whose writes it blocks — concerns that page and shows wherever the refusal applies, as the
  whole-subject state bullet below says.
- **At most two non-error banners appear on the whole rendered surface, including its shell and
  sections; error banners are the exception.** Error banners may coexist visibly with those status or action
  banners and with other independent error banners. For simultaneous non-error conditions, trace each
  to its state owner, writers and prerequisites. If they cannot legitimately coexist, fix the state
  or transition that produced them; a display selector does not repair it. If more than two legitimate
  non-error conditions require banners, surface the product or flow conflict and the concrete alternatives
  that would resolve it for the user's decision, under the global product-experience boundary. Preserve established banner
  rendering while that decision waits; combining messages, changing presentation, prioritizing,
  capping, hiding or dismissing an unresolved condition is not a repair. Continue independent
  authorized work. Verify an approved state or flow remedy at its producing transitions and on the
  whole resulting surface.
- **A refused or failed user action reports its reason beside what the reader is acting on, or
  through the existing bottom notification system.** A refusal that concerns what the reader
  entered or chose in a field or control — a choice the field cannot take, an amount over its limit
  — is that field's or control's inline error, in the page or dialog where they acted, and clears
  when they change it. Every other failed or refused save, submission, download or requested
  action, including one refused because of the account's or record's state or one taken from a
  status or error notice, reports its human-readable reason through the shared notification owner. Never add a page or dialog error
  banner or an error modal for a user-action failure, or create another notification stack.
  Classify the operation by its intent, not its status code, HTTP method or whether a button started
  it: loading or retrying the data a surface needs follows the resource-load rule below. Preserve
  entered values, the original notice and its state and remedy, and independent resource errors;
  the report neither clears nor replaces them. Release pending protection when the action
  settles and restore native retry controls according to their prerequisites. Keep the API's safe
  human reason, with the established generic fallback only when no safe reason is available.
- **One message carries one error.** A banner, an inline error and a notification each state a
  single problem; several problems are never joined into one string, list or summary in one
  surface. A field or control shows at most one inline error at a time — the first, when one action
  leaves it with several — while other fields each show their own. A form whose submission fails
  on several fields reports each on its field, never in one combined banner, and independent
  failures that each need a banner or notification get one each. A remedy that shows two problems
  by joining their messages is the same defect.
- **Present each failure once.** A terminal error message replaces content only when the whole
  page's subject is unavailable, not when one request or part of a usable page fails. This full-page
  exception owns the specific human-readable reason and recovery action, keeps usable navigation,
  and shows no banner repeating the same failure or second generic failure heading. Keep its purpose
  heading short; render the explanation and recovery instruction as normal body text, not as a large
  or bold heading containing the whole error message. Unrelated usable content stays available; its
  presence makes a partial resource failure use the shared error-banner route below instead.
  Independent action failures report as the user-action bullet above says.
- **Resource and data load failures on otherwise usable surfaces keep a persistent native error
  banner with retry, using the standard shared component's frame and error visual tone.** On a page,
  each failed resource appears in a dismissible banner in the page's shared error area at the top,
  outside its structural content. No feature-local or embedded partial surface renders error text, a banner or a
  terminal-error placeholder. Moving a native shared banner outside a panel while keeping it inside
  that feature's section, row or grid cell still violates this placement rule. Route every partial
  failure through the page's shared failure owner, preserve
  unrelated usable content, and identify the failed content and recovery action in that banner.
  Never substitute field error messages, a toast or an unframed row, or put the banner in a card,
  table row, field, footer, submit row or floating save panel. A dialog's data-load failure uses the
  native shared banner at the top of the dialog, above its fields, rather than moving it to the page
  behind the dialog. A dialog that only exists to say what an action needs first never opens on data
  it could not load: the load failure reports as a page resource failure, in the page's shared error
  banner, worded as an error rather than as the dialog's usual explanation. The banner
  never replaces the surface's own heading or description, which keep saying
  what the surface is while the banner says what went wrong.
  When a load failure appears or changes, keep entered values and reveal its banner through the
  existing shared failure owner if it is outside the visible scroll area, including inside a dialog. Do not
  scroll on ordinary edits or unrelated status changes. Verify the reader can see the explanation
  and recovery controls in the actual viewport; DOM presence or an alert role alone is not proof.
- **A state of the whole page's subject shows once, as a persistent banner at the top of the page.**
  An account, workspace or project that is suspended, archived or read-only is not a failure of any
  one section: no section repeats the state itself, and each shows what it still can. An actual
  failed data load still shows its standard error banner alongside the persistent state banner.
  A refused action reports as the user-action bullet above says, without replacing that state. A
  library card that has lapsed keeps its status banner when a loan request fails; the refusal
  appears as a notification.
- **Red is for errors and destructive actions, never required verification or another blocking status.**
  Red, or whatever tone the product reserves for destructive and
  failed states, marks only a failure, a refusal the product reports, or a destructive action: one
  that removes or discards what the reader cannot get back. A decision the reader makes on someone
  else's submission, such as rejecting or declining it, is not destructive; it takes the neutral
  tone and sits beside its counterpart, as reject directly under approve. A state that blocks or
  warns without being an error — something the reader must resolve, a hold, a limit reached — takes
  the warning tone, and a neutral status the neutral one, on a badge, a banner or a text color
  alike: an order waiting on a missing delivery address is a warning, not an error.
- A component that renders inside more than one shell — a widget in a canvas and on a page, a card
  in a list and alone — is checked in each one. Spacing that a parent supplies in one place and not
  the other is what a single screenshot cannot settle.

## Forms

- **Disable an action while locally known prerequisites are unmet.** Missing selections or incomplete
  required fields are normal editing state, not an error banner. Show errors for failures after a
  valid action or for failed data requests.
- **An action the reader cannot take is left out while another action beside it is available.**
  Cancelling a subscription that does not exist, "Mark all read" while nothing is unread, moving an
  item that has nowhere to go: shown disabled among working controls, each offers a press with no
  effect. An action with nothing to act on shows disabled only when no other action in its menu,
  toolbar or group is available, or when it is a paid control the plan bullet in **Layout And
  Spacing** locks to show what upgrading adds. An action whose prerequisite the reader can still
  meet stays, disabled, beside available actions, as the bullets here say: a form's submit while
  required fields are incomplete, Next until its step is complete, Save until something has changed,
  and an action while it is already running.
- **A form the product would refuse in full is never shown.** When every choice it offers would be
  refused, because the feature is off or nothing asked for is allowed, the page shows in its place
  why, and the way forward for this reader, with one action to leave. The server refuses that
  submission too, so the state cannot be reached by posting around the page.

- **A page or form that edits saved values saves through one floating save panel fixed to the bottom
  of the viewport, never through buttons on the page** — a settings page, a profile, a record's edit
  page alike. The panel is out of view until a field differs from its saved value; then it animates
  up from below the viewport's bottom edge to rest a little above it, holding a cancel action that
  restores the saved values and a save action. It floats over the page and never takes room in it,
  so nothing beneath it, a page footer included, moves when it rises. It stays in view as the reader
  scrolls while changes are unsaved, and slides away once they are saved or cancelled. A reader who
  unticks one topic on a newsletter preferences page sees it rise, and ticking the topic again sends
  it away. A save or reset button per section, a row of them at the end of the page or form, and a
  footer that sticks to the bottom of the page whether or not anything changed are the defect. A
  form that creates a record or submits a flow step is not editing saved values and keeps its own
  footer, and a form inside a dialog saves through the dialog's own actions; the panel belongs to a
  page the reader scrolls. One shared component owns the panel, under **Shared Surfaces**.
- **A form a person signs, certifies or attests to starts empty.** Nothing is seeded from a profile
  or an earlier submission, because the signer vouches for what they entered.
- **A form where the signed-in person enters someone else's details turns browser autofill off on
  every field, selects included** — a record made on another person's behalf, a person they add to a
  team, an organization or other record they name — so the browser never fills the reader's own
  name, address, email or saved organization into a record that is not the reader. One boundary
  around the form sets it for every control inside, including those a shared field component
  renders, never a token per field that the next added field forgets. "Off" means what the browser
  and the common password managers actually honour, which a bare `autocomplete="off"` is not for
  name, email and address fields. A search or picker box offers nothing the browser saved — neither
  saved details nor values typed into other fields — wherever it appears, since it never holds
  anyone's details: Chrome stops typed history only for exactly `off`, and fills nothing in a field
  it reads as a search term, so such a box takes `off` with a `search` name. The shared input and
  combobox components own those attributes. A form for the person's own details keeps accurate
  autocomplete tokens on each field.
- **A search box that picks a consequential record — a person, an account, a project — shows no
  suggestions and makes no request until the reader types.** A list on focus invites a pick by
  proximity rather than intent, and offers records the reader never asked to see. A picker over a
  low-stakes vocabulary, such as tags, may suggest on focus. The shared search component makes each
  caller declare which kind it picks rather than defaulting to either.
- **A suggestion list opens only once it has something to show:** its results, or its empty
  message once the search has finished. While the results for the typed text are still loading,
  the list stays closed and the field shows the loading state; an empty frame that grows when the
  results land reads as a broken list.
- **A form longer than a handful of fields is grouped into titled sections,** each holding the
  fields that answer one question; sibling forms share one section layout, under **Shared
  Surfaces** above. A section is never one per input: a control that only qualifies another — how
  picked items combine, the unit of an amount, the end of a range — sits in that control's section,
  directly under it, and the section's one description covers both.
- **Group fields by the question the reader answers, not by how short their values are.** Fields
  answered together sit side by side wherever the width allows, wrapping when it does not; independent
  decisions keep separate rows even when both controls are short.
- **A small setting that can be edited independently is edited where its value is shown.** Put the
  control beside its label or current value where space allows, sized for its values; stack it when
  narrow space or long labels need it, preserving readable values and the accessible label
  association. Opening another surface solely to change that one setting adds a step without a new
  decision. Keep a separate editing flow when coupled fields, detailed validation or sensitive-action
  confirmation require it, and retain the product's save and cancel behavior.
- **Comparable controls use comparable widths.** Inputs with the same role in a form take the same
  width or grid span; let the value format or available space justify a difference. A content-sized
  control beside a fixed-width peer reads as a different kind of choice even when both collect the
  same kind of answer.
- **One act gets one confirmation.** A single checkbox, worded as the whole statement the reader is
  making, stands for it; a second box restating part of the first asks twice.
- **Long fixed text a reader must accept — a certification, terms, a disclosure — is set in smaller
  muted type** and scrolls inside a maximum height as Layout And Spacing describes.
- **A placeholder shows a realistic example of the value's format,** such as `555-0100` or
  `2030-01-31`, never zeros, dots or a mask that reads as an existing value hidden from the reader.

## State and Hooks

- **A custom hook lives in its package's hooks area** — `hooks/`, or the repository's established
  hooks module — never inside a component or feature module, and a shared package exports it only
  once a consumer outside the package calls it.
- Prefix custom hooks with `use`, for example `useResources` or `useViewport`.
- Extract reusable logic into custom hooks

- Local state with `useState` for component-specific state
- Reuse the repository's established shared-state and server-state libraries instead of introducing parallel state layers.

- Use `useRef` for DOM access and mutable values
- Don't overuse refs for state that should cause re-renders

- Minimize useEffect usage - prefer derived state
- Always include dependencies
- Clean up subscriptions and timers

- Use `memo()` for expensive pure components
- Use `useMemo` for expensive computations
- Use `useCallback` for stable function references
- Don't over-memoize - profile first

## Rendering and Events

- Prefix with `handle`: `handleClick`, `handleSubmit`
- Use `useCallback` for handlers passed to memoized children
- **Every textual hyperlink has a visible, non-layout-shifting hover effect.** Its resting style
  already signals navigation; hovering changes its color or underline treatment with sufficient
  contrast. The shared link primitive owns that treatment where one exists; otherwise, use the
  product's link tokens consistently across tables, cards, and inline text.
- **Text on a clickable card, row or label stays selectable, and selecting it never activates the
  control.** A drag, double-click or triple-click that selects text leaves the checkbox or option as
  it was; only a plain click toggles it. Disabling selection to avoid the accidental toggle is the
  defect. The shared label component owns this, so every card and row built on it behaves the same.
- **A labelled button in a form, beside a field, or in a form's row of actions reads as a button at
  rest**: a filled surface, or a boundary with at least 3:1 contrast against what it sits on, plus
  a hover state. One that reads as text or a faint outline beside an input is the defect. A control
  may read as text only inside running text — a sentence, a hint, a field's description — where it
  takes the button component's link-style variant when it acts and is a link when it navigates.
  The call site picks a variant that reads as a button; a variant is restyled product-wide only
  where every use of it stands as such an action, and never with a class at one call site, as
  **Components and Props** says of every primitive.
- **A button is as wide as its label and padding, wherever it sits and at any viewport width.** One
  stretched to its row or container — a full-width class, a flex or grid child left to grow, a block
  display — reads as a bar rather than an action and is the defect. The button component keeps its
  own width in any parent, so no call site sets one, and buttons in a group each keep their own
  width; where they sit is **Layout And Spacing**'s to say. This holds over general advice to make
  components full width on small screens.
- **A button whose action is running is disabled, marked busy (`aria-busy`), and shows a spinner in
  place of its label at the same width**, so it cannot be pressed twice and nothing beside it moves.
  The label stays in the layout, transparent, holding the width and remaining the accessible name,
  with the spinner overlaid and hidden from assistive technology. The button component owns this
  behind one pending prop; there is no second label prop for the pending state ("Saving…").
  Pending covers only the time the reader waits on the product — preparing a window, saving a
  result. Once a dialog, window or connection flow the button opened is showing, the reader is
  acting rather than waiting, so the button stops spinning, and it spins again only for the work
  that follows when that flow returns.
- **Pressing a send action again moments later shows the same success as the first press.** A
  button that emails, notifies or reminds someone stays enabled once its request finishes, and the
  server sends nothing twice, as the HTTP rule's idempotent message operations say; a countdown, a
  "please wait" refusal or a disabled resend window in its place is the defect.

- Use ternary for simple conditions
- Use early return for complex conditions
- Avoid `&&` with numbers (renders 0)

```typescript
// Good
{count > 0 ? <Badge count={count} /> : null}

// Bad - renders "0" when count is 0
{count && <Badge count={count} />}
```

- Always provide stable `key` prop
- Don't use array index as key (unless list is static)
- Extract list items to separate components when complex

## Next.js App Router

Apply this section only when the repository uses the Next.js App Router.

### Project Structure and Routing

- `page.tsx` - Route pages
- `layout.tsx` - Shared layouts
- `loading.tsx` - Loading UI
- `error.tsx` - Error boundary
- `not-found.tsx` - 404 page, at the app root only; the root layout carries no navigation, so a
  missing page renders outside it, as the full-page message the page-layout bullet keeps for it
- `_components/` - Page-specific components

- Use `Link` from `next/link` for navigation
- Use `useRouter` for programmatic navigation
- Use `redirect()` in Server Components

### Rendering and Data

```typescript
// user-list.tsx - Server Component, no directive
export async function UserList() {
  const users = await fetchUsers(); // Direct DB/API access
  return <ul>{users.map(u => <li key={u.id}>{u.name}</li>)}</ul>;
}
```

```typescript
// search-input.tsx - Client Component, directive on the first line
"use client";

export function SearchInput() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  return <input value={query} onChange={e => setQuery(e.target.value)} />;
}
```

- **Render on the server.** A page, and every section of it that shows data, is an async Server Component that loads its data and renders it. A Client Component (`"use client"`) exists only for what the browser has to own — event handlers and input, state and effect hooks, browser-only APIs, a dialog, drag-and-drop, a third-party client widget — takes its data as props, and never fetches it.
- **Writes are Server Actions**, and Server Actions authenticate their caller and authorize what they read or change. A write re-renders the page when it finishes. A client-side data layer for reads — SWR, React Query, a fetching hook, a fallback cache seeded from the server — is the shape this replaces, not a companion to it, and a status that has to update live refreshes the server render on an interval instead of fetching on the client. A read that depends on input an open control holds in its own state — a city search as the reader types, a preview of the choices in a dialog — is a read-only Server Action that control calls, never a route handler it fetches; input that belongs in the address, such as a list's filters, stays search params the page renders from.
- **Expected refusals carry a specific, human-readable message the reader can act on**, worded as
  **Interface Copy** says. Trace generic copy for a known validation or business refusal to its service
  and fix that error contract there, rather than inventing replacement client copy. Expected
  refusals must not escape as internal server errors. Genuine 500 responses may keep a safe,
  generic message; diagnose and repair an unexpected 500 encountered during normal operation
  rather than accepting the failure feedback as a finished result. Clearly label failures deliberately
  induced to verify failure presentation so they cannot be mistaken for normal-flow defects.
- **Show the message the API sent.** Never key a table of your own copy off status codes for a first-party API: that is a second copy of its error vocabulary that nothing keeps in step, and it overrides the message the service chose. Wrong copy is fixed at the service that produced it.
- Keep one status-independent fallback for a response that carries no message at all, and reject a body that is a document rather than a message so a proxy's error page cannot reach the user as one.

### Metadata and Assets

Export metadata for SEO:

```typescript
export const metadata = {
  title: "Page title",
  description: "Page description",
};
```

Follow the repository's established image component and optimization policy consistently:

```typescript
<Image src="/logo.png" alt="Logo" width={100} height={50} />
```

### Environment

- `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` - exposed to client
- Other variables - server-only
- Never expose secrets with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix
